h1: Port, rum and wine cask finishes
title: Port, Rum and Wine Cask Finishes | Craft Beer School
desc: What port, rum and wine cask finishes add to a whisky, how a finish differs from full maturation and how to taste one honestly.
teaser: A finish is a whisky's last few months in a second cask. Port, rum and wine each leave a different mark.
standfirst: Cask finishing moves a mature whisky into a second cask for its final stretch. Here is what port, rum and wine casks tend to add and how to tell a finish that works from one that only adds colour.
sections: A finish is the last chapter, not the whole book

Most whisky spends its life in one kind of cask, usually American oak that once held bourbon. A finish moves that mature whisky into a different cask for a final period, often somewhere between a few months and two years. The idea is to add a layer on top of the spirit without rebuilding it.

That is different from full maturation in a wine cask, where the whisky spends its whole life there. Labels do not always make the difference clear. Words such as finished, double matured or extra matured usually point to a finish. Our guide to maturation and casks covers the main cask first.
Port casks add red fruit and colour

Port is a fortified wine from the Douro Valley in northern Portugal. Grape spirit is added partway through fermentation, which stops the yeast and leaves natural grape sugar behind. Ruby port is young, deep red and fruity. Tawny port spends longer in wood and turns nutty and amber.

A port cask finish usually shows up first in the glass: whisky with a pink or copper tint. On the nose expect red berries, plum and a jammy sweetness. On the palate port often softens a young spirit and rounds off the finish. The risk is a cloying whisky if the cask is very active or the finish runs too long.

Rum is distilled from sugar cane products, usually molasses or fresh cane juice. Casks that held rum, often ex-bourbon barrels re-used in the Caribbean, carry some of that sugar cane character back into whisky.

Expect banana, brown sugar, pineapple and a light toffee note. Rum casks rarely change colour much, so the effect is easy to miss if you are reading the glass rather than nosing it. They tend to suit lighter, fruity whiskies. Indian drinkers who grew up around dark molasses rum often spot the burnt sugar edge straight away.
Wine casks are the widest category

Wine cask covers almost anything, which is why it says so little on its own. A few common types:

  • Red wine casks, often from Bordeaux or similar regions, add red fruit, a dry tannic grip and colour.
  • Sweet white wine casks, such as Sauternes, add honey, apricot and a waxy richness.
  • Madeira and Marsala casks are fortified wines with a cooked, nutty, slightly sour tang that carries into the whisky.
  • Fresh red wine casks used without much rest can push a whisky towards sour or vinegary notes if the wine had any acetic character.

A good wine finish adds one clear idea. A poor one tastes like whisky and wine poured into the same glass.
How to judge a finish when you taste it

The honest test is to taste the finished whisky next to the same distillery's standard bottling if you can find one. That shows what the finish added and what it covered up.

  • Check the colour, then ignore it. A finish can tint a whisky in weeks.
  • Nose for the base spirit first. Can you still find the cereal, fruit or smoke underneath?
  • On the palate, ask whether the cask notes join the spirit or sit on top of it.
  • Wait for the finish. Wine casks often show a drying grip at the end.

Pour 15 ml, keep water on the table and spit when tasting more than two or three. A finish should make you want to go back to the glass. If the second sip tastes exactly like the first, the cask has done the talking.
Reading finish words on a label

Brands use a handful of phrases for the same idea. Finished in, double matured, extra matured and cask finish usually mean a second cask after a main period in another. Matured in, on its own, usually means the whole maturation happened in that cask type.

Look for two numbers if the label gives them: the total age and the length of the finish. A 12 year old whisky with six months in port is a very different thing from one that spent eight years in port. Plenty of labels give neither, which is legal and common.

The label also will not say whether the cask was first fill, meaning used for whisky for the first time after the wine, or refill. First fill casks give much more. That gap between what is printed and what is in the glass is why tasting matters more than reading.

Finishing lets a distiller give a familiar whisky a new face in months rather than years. That is useful for a range and for a brand that wants a festive or limited bottling. It also means the word finish can hide a young or ordinary spirit under a loud cask.

In Indian heat, where whisky matures faster and loses more to evaporation than in Scotland, a finish runs faster too. A few months in an active port cask in a hot warehouse can do what might take far longer in a cool one. That makes tasting and sampling the cask during the finish more important, not less.

Your first step: buy one finished whisky and taste it against an unfinished one of similar age. Write down only what the second cask added.
faqs: What is a cask finish in whisky?
A cask finish is a final period, often months to two years, in which a mature whisky rests in a second cask such as port, rum or wine to add an extra layer of flavour.
Does a port finish make whisky sweet?
It often adds red fruit and a softer, sweeter impression, but the whisky itself stays a spirit. Sweetness on the nose does not mean added sugar.
Is a finished whisky better than a standard one?
Not automatically. A finish suits some spirits and covers others. Tasting it next to the standard bottling is the best way to judge.
Why do some wine finishes taste sour?
Wine casks that held a wine with some acetic or sour character can pass a little of that to the whisky, especially in a long or very active finish.
